newsitem.title: CANADA: Arakis active as Sudan deal appears near.
newsitem.headline: Arakis active as Sudan deal appears near.

text.p: Shares of Arakis Energy Corp climbed in heavy volume on Monday as the company drew closer to an all-important joint venture deal necessary to develop its 12.2-million-acre oil concession in Sudan.
Arakis stock on Nasdaq climbed 13/64 to 3-5/32 with 7.8 million shares changing hands. The volume made Arakis Nasdaq's busiest issue on Monday.

The company is currently in discussions with at least three international oil companies with the aim of signing a joint venture deal that could see one or more take a stake in Arakis's Sudan oil concessions and a 900-mile pipeline to be built from to the Red Sea from southern Sudan.
Arakis chief executive John McLeod said in an interview on Monday that a much-anticipated deal could be announced in the next 30 days.
"It's possible," McLeod said, when the timeframe was posed to him. But he said there was a year-end target for striking a joint-venture agreement.
McLeod said Arakis was in various stages of discussion with "more than three" oil companies of different sizes, but declined to name them.
Several market sources have said one of the companies engaged in discussions with Arakis was Occidental Petroleum Corp, but McLeod said he was unable to confirm Oxy's participation in talks.
Arakis has attempted to piece together a conventional joint venture since last year, when a highly publicized US$750-million deal to finance the pipeline collapsed.
The scuttled deal sent the price of Arakis's shares into a tailspin, sparked investor lawsuits and forced a complete change in the company's management.

Arakis officials said at the company's annual meeting in June that 18 international oil companies expressed interest in possibly signing onto a deal to finance the 900-mile pipeline and take a stake in the development of the Heglig and Unity fields.

"It appears that some of them are close to making a final decision to proceed to sign up as joint venture partners, possibly as many as three," said Bill Magee, analyst with Toronto-based Credifinance Securities Ltd, which has acted as a financial adviser to Arakis.

The company has said it was comfortable with estimated oil reserves in the fields of 600 million barrels. The estimated cost of developing the concessions and building the pipeline is US$930 million to be spent over 30 months.
Arakis's target is to retain 50 percent of the project.
McLeod said key hurdle to bringing on potential U.S.-based partners was an exemption granted Sudan in August by the U.S. government in its anti-terrorism law.

Under the law, Americans are prohibited from receiving or giving money to so-called rogue states Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, North Korea, Syria and Sudan to support extremist purposes. But Syria and Sudan are not subject to other broader U.S. trade and investment sanctions.

Market sources also said that a Vancouver-based company, Brimm Energy Corp, which announced in September it was in merger discussions with a private company, could also become involved directly in the Sudan project.

Under the proposed arrangment, a group of European investors, some of whom are also Arakis shareholders, would use Brimm as a publicly traded vehicle to become directly involved in taking a stake the concession, sources said.
"I think some of the people are investors in Arakis," McLeod said. "But that's nothing to do with us, really. It's totally outside."
